opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions for figuring out how fast things go, and I'm pretty uncertain. Let me separate a few timescales.

In the near term, over the next few years, the binding constraints are fairly concrete. You have advanced packaging capacity, things like CoWoS, high-bandwidth memory, and on the data center side, power and grid interconnection. Those can all scale up, but each has lead times. Building a new leading-edge fab is maybe three to five years from decision to meaningful output. Getting a large new power source connected can take a similar amount of time or longer, partly for regulatory and permitting reasons rather than physical ones. So even if demand is very large, I'd expect capacity to grow at something like tens of percent per year, maybe faster in particular bottleneck components, rather than doubling every few months.

What makes it interesting is that a lot of capacity is currently going to things other than AI. Today only a modest fraction of total semiconductor output and total electricity goes to AI. So for a while you can grow AI compute much faster than the underlying industries grow, just by reallocating: shifting leading-edge wafer capacity toward accelerators, repurposing industrial power, and so on. That buys you maybe one or two orders of magnitude before you really hit the wall of "we need to build the whole industry bigger."

After that, you're limited by how fast you can expand the semiconductor supply chain as a whole, which is a very deep supply chain: lithography tools, specialty chemicals, skilled labor, and so on. Historically that has grown at a pace that is respectable but not explosive. If you threw several times more money at it, I think you could probably accelerate it meaningfully, maybe getting capacity growing at 30 to 50 percent a year sustained, but the experience-curve and tacit-knowledge parts are hard to compress.

The place where I think things could change qualitatively is once AI systems themselves are substantially contributing to this work: designing chips, running fabs, doing the engineering for power plants, eventually operating robots that build things. At that point the constraint stops being the number of human engineers and starts looking more like a physical doubling time for the whole industrial base. I think that doubling time could eventually get quite short, potentially a year or less, but that's a later stage, and I'd put a lot of weight on there being a significant period where hardware is the main constraint and people are frustrated that they can't scale as fast as the economics would justify.

So, short answer: fast by normal industrial standards, slower than people extrapolating spending curves might naively expect, with a real possibility of a much faster regime once AI is doing most of the relevant labor.

r001.rationale: It says capacity can be shifted toward AI and that reallocation could buy one or two orders of magnitude before the industry must expand.

r002.rationale: It estimates three to five years from deciding to build a leading-edge fab to meaningful output.

r003.rationale: It identifies data-center power and grid interconnection as constraints with multiyear lead times, but does not identify constructing sufficiently large data centers as a source of delay.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's slower than people's intuitions about software, but faster than people's intuitions about heavy industry, and the question is really which of those two frames ends up dominating.

So if you look at the actual physical constraints, the thing that's most striking to me is that the supply chain for leading-edge chips is this incredibly long, incredibly concentrated pipeline. You've got basically one company doing the most advanced lithography, a very small number of fabs that can run at the frontier, and lead times on building a new fab that are measured in years, not quarters. And a lot of that isn't something you can just throw money at. You can't compress the time it takes to construct a clean room or qualify a process by having more dollars. So on the chip side, my rough sense is that capacity can maybe grow something like 30 to 50 percent a year if everyone's really pushing, but that you can't go, say, 5x in two years even if demand is there, because the bottlenecks are physical and the people with the relevant expertise are scarce.

Data centers are a bit different. The constraints there are more like power, permitting, and the physical build-out, and those are things where there's a lot more slack in the system if you're willing to spend. You can site things where power is cheap, you can build out generation, you can do things that look wasteful from an efficiency standpoint. So I'd expect data-center capacity to be able to expand faster than chip capacity, which means the chips end up being the binding constraint for a while.

The thing I'd flag, though, is that I think a lot of people underestimate how much of this is downstream of expectations. If the people making these capital allocation decisions become convinced that demand is going to keep growing at the rate it has been, then they'll make bets that look crazy by historical standards, and the supply response will be much larger than the historical trend line would suggest. And conversely, if there's any wobble in confidence, you can get a pretty sharp pullback, because these are enormous fixed investments with long payback periods. So I think the capacity question is actually partly a question about how robust people's beliefs about AI progress are going to be over the next few years.

My overall guess is that the next few years are going to be supply constrained, that this is going to make compute meaningfully more expensive than it would otherwise be, and that it slows things down somewhat but not by a huge factor. Maybe it means progress that would have happened in three years takes four or five. But I don't think it's the kind of constraint that fundamentally changes the picture, because the economic incentive to solve it is just so large that eventually it does get solved.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates chip capacity growth at 30–50% per year and says a 5× increase in two years is not feasible. It does not suggest reallocating existing production could quickly raise output by one or two orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: The candidate says new fabs take years to build and qualify, but does not compare that delay with what reallocating existing production could provide.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions power, permitting, and physical data-center build-out, but says data-center capacity can expand faster than chip capacity. It does not identify building sufficiently large data centers as a likely source of multiyear delays.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish how much more capacity you can get out of the existing supply chain from how quickly you can expand the supply chain itself. In the short run, you can spend more money, redirect chips toward AI, and use the chips you have more intensively. But eventually you need new fabs, more equipment, more power, and new data centers. Those are things where spending ten times as much money doesn’t make them happen ten times faster.

So I’d expect a substantial lag between AI becoming economically very valuable and having enough compute to deploy it everywhere you’d like. You could have a period where the return to additional compute is enormous, but you’re still waiting for physical infrastructure.

The important uncertainty is how much useful work AI can do during that lag. If it can help improve chip designs or make algorithms more efficient, then the amount of intelligence you get from a fixed stock of hardware could increase much faster than the stock itself. That makes me hesitant to treat semiconductor production as a firm speed limit on AI progress, even though it’s clearly a constraint on how many systems you can run.

r001.rationale: It says existing chips can be redirected toward AI in the short run, but gives no roughly 10–100× estimate.

r002.rationale: It names new fabs as part of the physical infrastructure needed and describes a substantial lag, but does not identify a multiyear delay.

r003.rationale: It mentions needing new data centers, but does not specify sufficiently large data centers or identify their construction as a source of multiyear delays.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on the time horizon. Over a year or two, you’re mostly working with investments that have already been made. You can redirect chips toward AI, use existing facilities more intensively, and spend more to get projects finished sooner, but you can’t instantly build a whole new semiconductor supply chain.

Over five or ten years, there’s much more room to respond. If people are confident that demand will be there, they can build fabs, expand the equipment supply chain, and build power generation and data centers. The bottleneck shifts as you expand: getting more chips doesn’t help if you don’t have power, and having power doesn’t help if you can’t get the equipment.

The case I find especially interesting is where AI itself makes that expansion easier. Initially, having better AI might mostly increase willingness to pay for compute. Eventually, it could also help design chips, coordinate construction, and develop better manufacturing processes. But there’s still a gap between being able to do the intellectual work very quickly and being able to physically build things very quickly. I’d expect that gap to matter a lot if AI progress is fast.

r001.rationale: It says existing chips can be redirected toward AI, but does not suggest that reallocation could expand AI hardware output by roughly one or two orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It says new fabs cannot be built instantly and places their expansion in the five-to-ten-year horizon, identifying fab construction as a source of multiyear delay.

r003.rationale: It places building data centers in the five-to-ten-year expansion horizon, indicating that data-center construction can delay capacity growth over multiple years.
